explanations.explanation: Three thousand it is. Saul takes "…three thousand chosen men from all Israel…" and goes looking for David and his men (1 Samuel 24:2). That's a LOT of sandals on one dusty road. All that marching just to find David.

Close on the digits, friend, but the text says three thousand. Saul takes "…three thousand chosen men from all Israel…" (1 Samuel 24:2). You were off by a whole zero, and that zero is about twenty-seven hundred extra men.

Ten thousand would be a mighty big crowd, but the text says three thousand. Saul takes "…three thousand chosen men from all Israel…" (1 Samuel 24:2). Still plenty of men to go after David and his group.

David and his men, tucked back in the recesses of the cave (1 Samuel 24:3). Saul walks in, and the very men he's searching for are sitting back in the shadows. I think that's the quietest a group of grown men has ever been.

Saul did just come back from pursuing the Philistines (1 Samuel 24:1), so I see why that one came to mind. But the ones hiding in the cave are "…David and his men…" (1 Samuel 24:3). The Philistines aren't in this cave at all.

The text doesn't put anybody from Keilah in this scene. It says "…David and his men were hiding in the recesses of the cave." (1 Samuel 24:3). Saul went in to relieve himself, and the cave already had company in the back. I bet he came in expecting a quiet moment.

Enemy is right. David's men tell him, "This is the day about which the LORD said to you, ‘Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand…’" (1 Samuel 24:4). Then they urge David toward Saul. I think they were ready to start the celebration.

A kingdom is a big gift, but it isn't the word in the men's quote. They say the LORD told David, "Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand…" (1 Samuel 24:4). Swapping in kingdom is like tossing raisins in when the recipe calls for chocolate chips. Same batch, different ingredient.

Not people, friend. The words David's men repeat are, "Behold, I will deliver your enemy into your hand, that you may do with him as you wish." (1 Samuel 24:4). The LORD's words are about an enemy being handed over, and nobody else gets named. Put people in there and the whole line changes.

explanations.answer: Cuts off a corner of Saul's robe
explanations.explanation: David "…stealthily cut off a corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:4). It's a small snip, and it leads to a big moment. Keep an eye on that little piece of cloth, because it comes back.

explanations.answer: Takes the sword from Saul's side
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention Saul's sword in this scene. David "…stealthily cut off a corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:4). Just a snip of cloth.

explanations.answer: Unties the straps of Saul's sandals
explanations.explanation: No sandal straps here. The text says David "…stealthily cut off a corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:4). The robe is where all the action is.

Not quite, friend. The text says "Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:5). He didn't feel good about it. His conscience was stricken.
False is right. "Afterward, David’s conscience was stricken because he had cut off the corner of Saul’s robe." (1 Samuel 24:5). He didn't feel good about it. That tells you a lot about David.
Anointed is right. David says, "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." (1 Samuel 24:6). That's the reason he gives his men, plain and simple.

Servant is a fine word, and I'd happily wear it, but David doesn't use it here. He says, "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." (1 Samuel 24:6). That one word is the reason he gives for holding back.

Champion sounds mighty, like a trophy on a cookie contest shelf, but David picks a different word. He says, "May I never lift my hand against him, since he is the LORD’s anointed." (1 Samuel 24:6). Anointed is the reason he gives, plain and simple.

True, baker. Verse 7 says, "With these words David restrained his men, and he did not let them rise up against Saul." (1 Samuel 24:7). Those men had just said it was the day, and David still held them back. He did it with his words. Afterward, his own conscience was stricken just for cutting off the corner of Saul's robe.
Not false, friend. The text says "With these words David restrained his men, and he did not let them rise up against Saul." (1 Samuel 24:7). David stopped them with his words.

explanations.answer: Leaves the cave and goes on his way
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. "Then Saul left the cave and went on his way." (1 Samuel 24:7). He walks out while David is holding his men back. Quiet exit, and a corner of his robe is already gone (1 Samuel 24:4). Then David gets up, goes out of the cave, and calls out to him.

explanations.answer: Calls his chosen men into the cave
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Saul calls anybody in. It says "…Saul left the cave and went on his way." (1 Samuel 24:7). He just walks out.

explanations.answer: Lies down to sleep in the cave
explanations.explanation: No nap for Saul. The text says "…Saul left the cave and went on his way." (1 Samuel 24:7). With David's men in the back, a nap would have been quite the plot twist.

First David calls out, "My lord the king!" Then David "…bowed facedown in reverence" (1 Samuel 24:8). He greets the king who has been hunting him (1 Samuel 24:11) with a bow. That tells you what's in his heart toward Saul.
The text has no sword in David's hand here. It says "…David bowed facedown in reverence" (1 Samuel 24:8). He greets the king with a bow.
David doesn't run. He walks out and "…bowed facedown in reverence" (1 Samuel 24:8). He's done hiding for this conversation.
Harm is right. David asks, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ‘Look, David intends to harm you’?" (1 Samuel 24:9). He's asking Saul to think about who he's listening to.

Mock is a sneaky guess, but it's not the word David uses. He asks, "Why do you listen to the words of men who say, ‘Look, David intends to harm you’?" (1 Samuel 24:9). The charge is that David wants to harm Saul, and he's asking why Saul listens to the men saying it.

Desert fits the wilderness setting, but it doesn't show up in David's question. He says, "Look, David intends to harm you…" (1 Samuel 24:9). Harm is what the men are accusing him of, and David is asking why Saul listens.
True. David says, "I was told to kill you, but I spared you…" (1 Samuel 24:10). He says it right to the king's face. I think that's honest about how close it got.
Not false, friend. David tells Saul, "I was told to kill you, but I spared you…" (1 Samuel 24:10). He's being honest about how close it got.

Rebellion is right. David says, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). Just before that he tells Saul, "…look at the corner of your robe in my hand." So the robe corner is his proof.

Fear isn't in that sentence, though it'd be a natural guess for a man hiding in a cave. David says, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). Evil and rebellion are the two things he says aren't in his hands.

Pride isn't the word here. David says, "Know and see that there is no evil or rebellion in my hands." (1 Samuel 24:11). He's answering the charge that he intends harm, so evil and rebellion are the two he names.

Not quite, friend. David says, "May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you." (1 Samuel 24:12). He leaves the judging to the LORD.

False is right. David says, "May the LORD judge between you and me, and may the LORD take vengeance on you, but my hand will never be against you." (1 Samuel 24:12). He puts it in the LORD's hands, not his own.

explanations.answer: A dead dog and a flea
explanations.explanation: A dead dog and a flea. David asks, "Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea?" (1 Samuel 24:14). He's calling himself small. I've been called a lot of things in my day, but never a flea.
Those are big, scary animals, and David doesn't use them here. He asks, "Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea?" (1 Samuel 24:14). A dead dog and a flea are what he names. Not a lion in sight.
Those are gentle little creatures, but David doesn't name them. He asks, "Whom are you pursuing? A dead dog? A flea?" (1 Samuel 24:14). He's making himself sound small.

Saul's hand. David says, "May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15). He's asking the LORD to plead his case. He's talking to Saul, so "your hand" is Saul's.

The Philistines don't come up in David's words here. He says, "May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15). David is speaking to Saul, so "your hand" is Saul's.
David's men aren't named in those words. He says, "May He take notice and plead my case and deliver me from your hand." (1 Samuel 24:15). He's speaking to Saul, so "your hand" is Saul's.
Son is right. Saul calls back, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). David said "my father," and Saul answers with "my son."
Servant isn't what Saul says. He calls out, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). He calls David his son, and that comes right after David called him "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11).
Friend is a nice word, but Saul uses a different one. He calls out, "Is that your voice, David my son?" (1 Samuel 24:16). David had said "my father" (1 Samuel 24:11), and Saul answers with "my son."

explanations.answer: You are more righteous than I
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. Saul tells David, "You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil." (1 Samuel 24:17). That's a hard thing for anyone to say out loud.

explanations.answer: You have fooled me once again
explanations.explanation: Saul doesn't say that. After weeping, he says, "You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil." (1 Samuel 24:17). He admits David has treated him with good. That's the opposite of calling David a fooler.
That's not what Saul says here. He says, "You are more righteous than I, for you have rewarded me with good, though I have rewarded you with evil." (1 Samuel 24:17). It's the opposite of that.
True. Saul says, "May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me this day." (1 Samuel 24:19). Those are his exact words to David. He's asking the LORD to reward David with good.

Not false, friend. Saul really does say, "May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done for me this day." (1 Samuel 24:19). He's asking the LORD to reward David with good. It's right there in the verse.

King is right. Saul says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands." (1 Samuel 24:20). He says it himself, right there in the wilderness.

Priest? Friend, I've seen priests in cookie-box stories, and nobody here is measuring David for a priest's robe. Saul says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands." (1 Samuel 24:20). Saul is the sitting king, and he just handed his own job title to the man he's been chasing. I think that line cost him a lot to say.

Judge sounds official, but it isn't what Saul says. He says, "Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established in your hands." (1 Samuel 24:20). The word is king, and the kingdom of Israel goes with it.

explanations.answer: Not to cut off his descendants
explanations.explanation: That's what Saul asks. He says, "…swear to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house." (1 Samuel 24:21). It's a request about his family line.

explanations.answer: Never to come near his house
explanations.explanation: Saul doesn't ask for that. He says, "…swear to me by the LORD that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house." (1 Samuel 24:21). It's about his descendants and his name.

explanations.answer: To fight the Philistines for him
explanations.explanation: The Philistines don't come up in Saul's request. He asks David to swear "…that you will not cut off my descendants or wipe out my name from my father’s house." (1 Samuel 24:21). It's about his family line, not a battle.
Not so, friend. The text says "…David gave his oath to Saul." (1 Samuel 24:22). He didn't refuse. He gave it.
False is right. "…David gave his oath to Saul." (1 Samuel 24:22). He gave Saul what he asked for. Saul had asked for that oath in the verse before (1 Samuel 24:21).
Up to the stronghold. "…Saul returned home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). They each go their own way. Saul heads home while David and his men climb up.
Keilah isn't named here. The text says "…David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). Saul is the one heading home.
The cave is behind them now. The text says "…David and his men went up to the stronghold." (1 Samuel 24:22). They go up higher.
